notes.summary: Coding-Decoding tests whether you can work out the rule a 'code language' uses to change letters, numbers or words, and then apply it to a new word. SSC CGL usually sets 2-3 questions per paper. Most are letter shifts, opposite letters, reversals, position-value codes and sentence (common-word) codes.
keyPoints: Learn letter positions using EJOTY as anchors: E = 5, J = 10, O = 15, T = 20, Y = 25. Then R = 18 and W = 23 come instantly.
Reverse position = 27 − normal position: A = 26, M = 14, Z = 1.
Opposite letter pairs add up to 27: A-Z, B-Y, C-X, D-W, E-V, F-U, G-T, H-S, I-R, J-Q, K-P, L-O, M-N.
Write the shift under each letter of the example (+1, +2, +3, +4 or +1, −1, +1, −1). The pattern is in the shifts, not in the letters.
Wrap around after Z: Z + 1 = A, A − 1 = Z, and W + 6 = C (23 + 6 = 29, 29 − 26 = 3).
Structural codes: the whole word reversed, each half reversed (MOTHER → TOMREH), adjacent pairs swapped (PRINTER → RPNIETR), or the first and last letters swapped with the inner letters changed.
Number codes can be the sum of positions (CAT = 24), the product (CAT = 60), squares (ACE = 1-9-25), or sum × number of letters (PEN = 35 × 3 = 105).
Sentence coding: compare two sentences. The word they share has the code they share. Use a third sentence to pin down the word that is left.
Substitution codes ('water is called air'): the answer is the code word for the real answer, not the real word itself.
traps: Checking the rule on only the first one or two letters. Always verify it on every letter of the example.
Forgetting to wrap around, for example writing A − 1 as anything other than Z.
In substitution questions, answering with the real-world word (water) instead of its code name (air).
Mixing up sum and product in number codes: DOG is 26 by sum but 420 by product.
notes.examTip: Write the positions of the example word and its code side by side and look at the differences. Most SSC codes show their rule within 20 seconds this way.

questions.text: In a certain code language, GOLD is written as TLOW. How will SILK be written in that language?
questions.explanation:
Each letter is replaced by its opposite letter (the two positions add up to 27): G(7) → T(20), O(15) → L(12), L(12) → O(15), D(4) → W(23).
SILK: S(19) → H(8), I(9) → R(18), L(12) → O(15), K(11) → P(16).
So SILK is written as HROP.

questions.text: In a certain code language, PENCIL is written as ODMBHK. How will ERASER be written in that language?
questions.explanation:
Each letter moves one place back: P → O, E → D, N → M, C → B, I → H, L → K.
ERASER: E → D, R → Q, A → Z (wrap around), S → R, E → D, R → Q.
So ERASER is written as DQZRDQ.

questions.text: In a certain code language, TABLE is written as ELBAT. How will CHAIR be written in that language?
questions.explanation:
The letters are written in reverse order: T-A-B-L-E becomes E-L-B-A-T.
CHAIR reversed is R-I-A-H-C.
So CHAIR is written as RIAHC.

questions.text: In a certain code, BAD is written as 7 and FED is written as 15. How will CAGE be written in that code?
questions.explanation:
The code is the sum of the letter positions: BAD = 2 + 1 + 4 = 7 and FED = 6 + 5 + 4 = 15.
CAGE = 3 + 1 + 7 + 5 = 16.

questions.text: If 'sky' is called 'sea', 'sea' is called 'water', 'water' is called 'air' and 'air' is called 'cloud', then where do fish live?
questions.explanation:
In reality, fish live in water.
In this code, 'water' is called 'air'.
So the answer is 'air'.

questions.text: In a certain code, GIVE is written as 5137 and BAT is written as 924. How will GATE be written in that code?
questions.explanation:
Match the letters to the digits in order: G = 5, I = 1, V = 3, E = 7 (from GIVE) and B = 9, A = 2, T = 4 (from BAT).
GATE = G, A, T, E = 5, 2, 4, 7.
So GATE is written as 5247.

questions.text: In a certain code language, MOTHER is written as TOMREH. How will FATHER be written in that language?
questions.explanation:
Split the word into two halves and reverse each half: MOT | HER → TOM | REH.
FATHER: FAT | HER → TAF | REH.
So FATHER is written as TAFREH.

questions.text: In a certain code language, WATER is written as XZUDS. How will RIVER be written in that language?
questions.explanation:
The shifts alternate +1, −1: W + 1 = X, A − 1 = Z, T + 1 = U, E − 1 = D, R + 1 = S.
RIVER: R + 1 = S, I − 1 = H, V + 1 = W, E − 1 = D, R + 1 = S.
So RIVER is written as SHWDS.

questions.text:
In a certain code language:
'pin ta lo' means 'sweet hot tea'
'ta mu pin' means 'cold sweet tea'
'lo zu mu' means 'hot cold coffee'
What is the code for 'coffee'?
questions.explanation:
Sentences 1 and 3 share only the word 'hot' and only the code 'lo', so lo = hot.
Sentences 2 and 3 share only the word 'cold' and only the code 'mu', so mu = cold.
In sentence 3, the remaining word 'coffee' must have the remaining code.
So coffee = zu.

questions.text: In a certain code, CAT is written as 60 and BAG is written as 14. How will DOG be written in that code?
questions.explanation:
The code is the product of the letter positions: CAT = 3 × 1 × 20 = 60 and BAG = 2 × 1 × 7 = 14.
DOG = 4 × 15 × 7 = 60 × 7 = 420.
(26 is the sum of the positions, a common slip.)

questions.text: In a certain code, CAB is written as 24-26-25. How will FADE be written in that code?
questions.explanation:
Each letter is coded by its position counted from Z (reverse position = 27 − normal position): C = 27 − 3 = 24, A = 26, B = 25.
FADE: F = 27 − 6 = 21, A = 26, D = 27 − 4 = 23, E = 27 − 5 = 22.
So FADE is written as 21-26-23-22.

questions.text: In a certain code, ACE is written as 1-9-25. How will BIG be written in that code?
questions.explanation:
Each letter is coded as the square of its position: A = 1² = 1, C = 3² = 9, E = 5² = 25.
BIG: B = 2² = 4, I = 9² = 81, G = 7² = 49.
So BIG is written as 4-81-49.

questions.text: In a certain code language, PRINTER is written as RPNIETR. How will MONITOR be written in that language?
questions.explanation:
The letters are swapped in adjacent pairs, and the last letter of an odd-length word stays where it is: PR → RP, IN → NI, TE → ET, R stays.
MONITOR: MO → OM, NI → IN, TO → OT, R stays.
So MONITOR is written as OMINOTR.

questions.text: In a certain code language, LAMP is written as QNBM. How will DESK be written in that language?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: move each letter one place forward, so LAMP → MBNQ.
Step 2: reverse the result, so MBNQ → QNBM.
DESK → EFTL (each letter +1) → reversed, LTFE.
So DESK is written as LTFE.

questions.text: In a certain code language, DOG is written as TLW. How will CAT be written in that language?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: replace each letter by its opposite letter: D → W, O → L, G → T, giving WLT.
Step 2: reverse it: WLT → TLW.
CAT: C → X, A → Z, T → G, giving XZG, which reversed is GZX.
So CAT is written as GZX.

questions.text:
In a certain code language:
'134' means 'good and tasty'
'478' means 'see good pictures'
'729' means 'pictures are faint'
Which digit stands for 'see'?
questions.explanation:
Statements 1 and 2 share only the word 'good' and only the digit 4, so 4 = good.
Statements 2 and 3 share only the word 'pictures' and only the digit 7, so 7 = pictures.
In statement 2, '478' = 'see good pictures', so the remaining digit 8 = see.

questions.text: In a certain code, PEN is written as 105 and INK is written as 102. How will BOOK be written in that code?
questions.explanation:
PEN: 16 + 5 + 14 = 35, and 35 × 3 (the number of letters) = 105.
INK: 9 + 14 + 11 = 34, and 34 × 3 = 102.
So code = (sum of positions) × (number of letters).
BOOK: 2 + 15 + 15 + 11 = 43, and 43 × 4 = 172.

questions.text: In a certain code language, GARDEN is written as FBQCFM. How will MOBILE be written in that language?
questions.explanation:
Consonants move one place back and vowels move one place forward: G → F, A → B, R → Q, D → C, E → F, N → M.
MOBILE: M (consonant) → L, O (vowel) → P, B → A, I (vowel) → J, L → K, E (vowel) → F.
So MOBILE is written as LPAJKF.

questions.text: In a certain code language, KEYBOARD is written as DSBPCZFK. How will DISTANCE be written in that language?
questions.explanation:
The first and last letters swap places (K ... D becomes D ... K).
The six inner letters E Y B O A R each move +1 (F Z C P B S) and are then written in reverse order (S B P C Z F).
DISTANCE: the first letter D and last letter E swap, giving E ... D.
Inner letters I S T A N C → +1 → J T U B O D → reversed → D O B U T J.
So DISTANCE is written as EDOBUTJD.

questions.text: In a certain code language, MIRROR is written as NKUVTX. How will WINDOW be written in that language?
questions.explanation:
The shift grows by one with each letter: M + 1 = N, I + 2 = K, R + 3 = U, R + 4 = V, O + 5 = T, R + 6 = X.
WINDOW: W + 1 = X, I + 2 = K, N + 3 = Q, D + 4 = H, O + 5 = T, W + 6 = C (23 + 6 = 29, and 29 − 26 = 3 = C).
So WINDOW is written as XKQHTC.
